rows.question: Is the non-refundable security deposit in this agreement legally enforceable in India?

chroma.answer: No, the clause stating the security deposit is "NON-REFUNDABLE" and "shall stand forfeited to the Lessor in all circumstances whatsoever, including normal expiry of the lease" (as per Clause 3 of your Rental Deed) is unlikely to be fully enforceable as written under Indian law. In India, courts treat such clauses, if they are essentially a penalty, as subject to the principles of liquidated damages. While parties can agree on a fixed sum for a breach, courts will only award reasonable compensation up to that amount and will not enforce it if it is deemed a penalty. Forfeiting the entire deposit even upon normal expiry of the lease, without any actual loss to the Lessor, would likely be considered a penalty rather than reasonable compensation, and thus may not be upheld by a court. This is grounded in the principles of Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as explained in the definition of "Liquidated damages".

qdrant.answer: While the Rental Deed states in Clause 3 that the security deposit of Rs. 6,60,000 is "NON-REFUNDABLE and shall stand forfeited to the Lessor in all circumstances whatsoever, including normal expiry of the lease," its legal enforceability in India is subject to scrutiny. Indian law views such pre-determined sums, if they function as a penalty, differently than a genuine pre-estimate of damages. As per the definition of Liquidated damages (referencing Section 74, Indian Contract Act, 1872), courts in India award only reasonable compensation up to the agreed amount and will not enforce the sum if it is determined to be a penalty. Therefore, despite the clause, a court may not enforce the forfeiture of the entire deposit if it is deemed a penalty rather than a reasonable pre-estimate of actual loss, or if it is forfeited even upon normal expiry without actual damages to the Lessor.

rows.question: Is the penalty of paying the entire balance rent for early termination valid under Indian law?

chroma.answer: Under the rental deed, if the Lessee vacates before the 36-month lock-in period for any reason, they are liable to pay the entire balance rent for the unexpired period immediately, described as liquidated damages, in addition to forfeiting the security deposit. While the contract specifies this amount as liquidated damages, Indian law, specifically Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as noted in the definition of 'Liquidated damages' and the 'Red flag: Excessive liquidated damages / penalty' context, states that courts will only award reasonable compensation up to the amount stipulated, and will not enforce it if it is truly a penalty far exceeding genuine loss. Therefore, while the clause exists in the deed, a court under Indian law would likely only award a 'reasonable compensation' for the breach, rather than the full unexpired rent if it is deemed excessive.

rows.question: Can the landlord increase the rent at his sole discretion as clause 2 of this deed says?

chroma.answer:
Yes, according to Clause 2 of the Rental Deed, the Lessor (landlord) *may* revise the rent upward at his sole discretion at any time by giving 7 days notice. The Lessee (tenant) explicitly agrees to have no right to object to or contest such a revision.

However, it is important to note that a clause granting one party a unilateral right to modify terms, such as revising rent at their sole discretion, is identified as a high-risk "red-flag clause." Such clauses are risky because they allow one party to alter key terms without the other's consent. Under Indian law, this type of provision may be considered an "unfair contract" as per Section 2(46) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
